item.title: Democrats Nominate Jeffries as Speaker, Making History
item.description:
House Democrats on Wednesday nominated Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York to be speaker, voting overwhelmingly over resistance from the left to put him in line to become the first Black lawmaker to hold the post.

The election by secret ballot came just over two weeks after Mr. Jeffries, 56, who has led House Democrats since 2022, presided over sweeping victories for his party, which won a historically large majority in the midterm elections.

The vote was 251 to 11, with two Democrats abstaining, according to a person who attended the confidential session and detailed the results on the condition of anonymity. The margin demonstrated the breadth of Mr. Jeffries’s backing in a large and ideologically diverse caucus.

Accepting the nomination, he paid homage to the civil rights hero and long-serving Representative John Lewis of Georgia, who frequently exhorted people to get in “good trouble” fighting injustice.

“It’s a ‘good trouble’ moment in America,” Mr. Jeffries told the assembled Democrats.

He will still have to be elected on the House floor in January, when he will need a majority of members in the chamber to rise and say his name to formally win the post that is second in line to the presidency. But the lopsided secret-ballot vote suggested he will have more than enough support to do so.

Mr. Jeffries’s nomination was almost a foregone conclusion; no Democrat emerged to challenge him, and even some of his loudest critics ultimately did not want to publicly oppose the man in line to be the nation’s first Black speaker.

His frictionless ascent counted as a rarity in the House, where party leaders often rise through tumultuous challenges.

“It’s a good day,” said Representative Steny Hoyer of Maryland, the former No. 2 Democrat, as he headed into the closed-door session. “I served with the first woman speaker of the House. Now we’re going to elect the first African American speaker of the House.” Mr. Hoyer said it was a testimony to the country’s progress.

Inside the room, according to a person who was present, Representative James E. Clyburn, Democrat of South Carolina, gave the final speech nominating Mr. Jeffries, invoking Mr. Lewis, who died in 2020, as he reflected on the significance of elevating a Black man for the job.

Still, Mr. Jeffries faced loud grass-roots resistance from progressives fed up with the Democratic Party establishment who see Mr. Jeffries, a reserved moderate and prodigious fund-raiser, as an avatar of the status quo who is beholden to corporate interests.

Progressives who want Democrats to cut off U.S. aid to Israel and who champion “Medicare for all” said they were concerned that Mr. Jeffries, a longtime supporter of the Jewish state who they view as too closely aligned with AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group, would stand in the way of their demands.

In a statement, a group of newly elected democratic socialist lawmakers said they voted against Mr. Jeffries because their constituents sent them to Congress with a “mandate” to deliver change on “Medicare for all, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics” and “ending the genocide in Gaza.” While the group acknowledged some “meaningful progress” in their conversations with Mr. Jeffries, they said they still opposed him.

The group included Representatives-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York; Adam Hamawy of New Jersey; Frederick Haynes of Texas; Melat Kiros of Colorado; Donavan McKinney of Michigan; and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.

Mr. Jeffries, who in recent days met with almost all members and newly elected Democrats as he sought to wrap up his nomination with as little opposition as possible, is known for his cautious and highly disciplined style.

He likes to host listening sessions and have a caucus “family discussion” before telegraphing his stance on any issue. But he also appears willing to move in response to broad calls for bold action.

On Tuesday, for instance, less than 24 hours before his nomination, Mr. Jeffries endorsed a broad expansion of Medicare to cover more Americans and a wider variety of services, edging closer to the Medicare for all proposal championed by progressives.

It was a sign that with a larger majority giving him more room to maneuver and progressives pressing him to take up a bolder agenda, he saw the need and opportunity to take a more ambitious approach.

Mr. Jeffries, who grew up in a working-class home in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn in the 1980s, first ran for the State Legislature at 29. He was always viewed by people around him as a potential national leader, though he had been hesitant to reflect on the significance of his place in history until he had the vote wrapped up.

“Over the last four years, that pressure has already been on me,” he said in an interview earlier this month, when asked if he felt the weight of breaking a racial barrier. “Failure is not an option.”

Despite the sweeping electoral victories, Mr. Jeffries has been facing loud resistance to his leadership. Many lawmakers said their phone lines had been blowing up with constituents demanding a new face to lead the party as it takes control of Congress. But even amid that pressure, many of the progressives in Congress said they thought Mr. Jeffries deserved a chance to lead them in the majority.

item.title: The Anti-A.I. Campus Movement Is Growing
item.description:
Last March, a handful of students at Transylvania University created a petition, attempting to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus. It asked the administration to cancel chatbot licenses with A.I. giants and instead invest the money in “human-centered education.”

About a third of the college’s students signed on.

Transylvania, in Lexington, Ky., is tiny, with under 1,000 students. But across the country and the globe, there has been a swell of campus resistance to A.I., including a growing group of conscientious objectors who refuse to use A.I. at all.

Polls show the vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work. College leaders have generally embraced A.I., saying it is key to preparing students for the work force.

But as A.I. use grows, more students and faculty are sounding alarms and trying to slow it down.

Much of the opposition comes from the political left, and focuses on how A.I. could harm the environment, diminish the power of workers or be used in warfare. Some of the loudest voices in opposition are studying the arts, where human creativity is paramount, or the law, as tech companies face lawsuits over potential copyright and privacy violations.

But there are also deep concerns that A.I. degrades the experience of college itself, by removing the productive struggle of learning.

Resistors from California to Sydney to Paris are increasingly publishing manifestoes that lay out demands: that colleges not partner with A.I. companies; that professors not be required to use generative A.I. in lessons or grading; and that students be allowed to refuse to complete assignments that require the use of chatbots, without any impact on their grades.

At the University of Kentucky, a research employee who described himself as a humanist successfully applied for a religious exemption from using A.I.

Alice Beatty, 22, helped lead the Transylvania petition drive as a senior last spring. The student newspaper had called attention to the $120,000 the university paid to purchase licenses to ChatGPT and Gemini, chatbots from OpenAI and Google. And Ms. Beatty had participated in a discussion group formed by several A.I.-skeptical professors.

She noted that even before Transylvania provided free access to chatbots, A.I. had been everywhere on campus. Students used it to summarize readings, break down physics problems and compose discussion-board posts and papers that they were supposed to be writing the old-fashioned way, on their own.

Yet when Ms. Beatty and some classmates stood near the dining hall to collect signatures on the petition, almost everyone they spoke to signed.

“I use A.I.,” she recalled some peers telling her, “and I am ashamed I use it.”

A spokeswoman for Transylvania University declined an interview request but said that professors were free to either embrace A.I., limit its use or ban it entirely in their classes.

For students, ethical and practical questions about A.I. will be part of the world they enter after graduating, she said by email.

Vague and confusing college A.I. policies have helped create the conscientious objector movement, said Hollis Robbins, an English professor at the University of Utah who writes often about A.I. and education. She suggested that colleges stop grading take-home assignments that are easy to cheat on with A.I., and shut down online courses that have become rife with academic misconduct in the A.I. era.

If institutions took those steps, she argued, students might be more curious and hopeful about the technology.

“There is silence about these major tech issues,” she said. “Students just seeing grown-ups being inconsistent and letting them down.”

Georgetown University began offering students and faculty free access to Gemini in March. At the time, like many institutions, Georgetown generally allowed each professor to set their own A.I. rules.

Yet in focus groups on A.I. conducted by the university, students asked for clearer guidance. They were worried about cognitive offloading, cheating and A.I. providing false information. Forty percent of the student sentiment was cautious or negative toward A.I., according to the university, compared with 25 percent that was positive or hopeful.

Georgetown’s student newspaper published an editorial criticizing the Gemini license, arguing that it tacitly pushed students toward technology that is often used to plagiarize and avoid academic effort.

This fall, the university is changing its approach. Under a new president, Eduardo M. Peñalver, it announced it would form a faculty committee to come up with clearer principles on A.I. use. For Georgetown, a Jesuit institution, Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical on the risks of A.I. will be an important influence.

Dr. Peñalver said in an interview that Georgetown would seek to make course expectations around A.I. more transparent and provide more tech-free spaces on campus. Oral presentations, discussion groups and in-person tests would become more important, he said, to protect “from the intrusion of this technology.”

Still, the university will continue to expand free access to A.I. tools, which he said had the potential to do good.

“We’re not interested in pushing people to use A.I. in ways that don’t align with their values,” Dr. Peñalver said. “But I certainly encourage people to learn about it.”

“Even if you’re opposed to this technology,” he added, “that awareness and understanding is important to the success of your project.”

Many conscientious objectors, though, say they try to avoid generative A.I. as much as possible, blocking it from their devices and not experimenting with it in their own work.

Emily Tucker, executive director of the Center on Privacy and Technology at Georgetown Law School, has been a leader in organizing resistance to A.I. use on campus. She has also signed an open letter with 1,300 other educators “who refuse the call for generative A.I. adoption in schools and colleges, and reject the narrative of its inevitability.”

Law students have told her they feared that if they didn’t use A.I. to speed their output, they would be outpaced in class and at work by those who did. But Professor Tucker said that using A.I. degrades a student’s ability to read and analyze dense legal texts, and risks incorrect citations of case law.

“It’s not useful,” said Professor Tucker, who said she rarely uses A.I. herself, though she acknowledged it might help in some tasks, like seeking specific information within a large set of documents.

At Cornell, Shimon Edelman, a psychology professor who holds a Ph.D. in computer science, has also signed the anti-A.I. letter. He lets students decide whether or not to use A.I., though he warns them it could degrade deeper learning.

He said he had been dismayed to see the Cornell administration greet A.I. warmly, as an “essential tool,” instead of warning more forcefully against its risks. In October, Cornell announced free access to chatbots, A.I. coding tools and agentic A.I.

“It’s unthinkable,” Professor Edelman said of using A.I. in his own research, even when he faced having to read 800 documents for a recent book project.

Emmali Simmelink, a senior studying classics and religion at Whitman College in Washington State, said students on her campus sometimes plug classroom discussion prompts directly into ChatGPT.

“If you can’t generate a coherent thought without ChatGPT, I genuinely lose a lot of respect for you,” she said. She added, laughing, “I am really insufferable about this.”

She said she brings up concerns about the environmental impact of A.I. as soon as she hears somebody say, “I asked ChatGPT.”

The topic can be divisive socially, so much so, several students said, that friend groups often develop a shared view of A.I.

Preston Hicks, 26, is studying history and education at Rider University in New Jersey — a second degree, after he worked previously as a software developer. He said many of his friends are artists who instinctually oppose A.I., a view he often shares.

But he can also imagine using A.I. in his future career as a teacher, to handle paperwork and other logistical tasks.

“I am more nuanced,” he said. “If I see a good use, I will use it.”

item.title: Trump Grows Frustrated With Vance Over Iran War Critique
item.description:
At first, President Trump appeared notably unfazed by Vice President JD Vance’s post-election analysis blaming the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.

“I think it’s largely true,” the president told reporters after Mr. Vance posted a lengthy missive on social media in which he also critiqued much of the administration’s messaging in the run-up to the elections.

But over the past two weeks, Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how his vice president framed his assessment of what went wrong, complaining to aides and allies that Mr. Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran, according to people with knowledge of the president’s comments.

At the same time, Mr. Trump has continued to praise Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, in private conversations and suggesting that he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe discussions going on behind closed doors. Mr. Trump’s allies have noted that Mr. Rubio has repeatedly said the president’s move to attack Iran was essential for the country’s national security.

Mr. Trump has hinted at his irritation with Mr. Vance in public, saying earlier this month that the vice president should have “made one other statement.”

“If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes,” he said, laying out what he believes was missing from Mr. Vance’s analysis.

The tension comes at a critical juncture for Mr. Vance, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028, a campaign in which Mr. Trump’s support could be critical to his ability to secure the Republican nomination. The president’s favorable comments about Mr. Rubio are the latest example of how Mr. Trump has been weighing the strengths of the two men as the question of his successor grows more urgent.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Mr. Vance’s office declined to comment, pointing to recent interviews the vice president has given.

When asked on Fox News this week about his post-election commentary and whether there was any “daylight” between him and the president, Mr. Vance said, “I think there’s no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration.”

On Wednesday, Mr. Vance canceled a planned appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit, citing meetings in Washington to address the recent tech outages.

Since Mr. Trump brought him aboard as his running mate for a second term, many Republicans have assumed that Mr. Vance, a former senator from Ohio, would be the front-runner for their party’s nomination in 2028. But Mr. Trump has waffled publicly and privately on his vice president throughout his tenure, and Mr. Vance says he has not decided whether to run for president.

“I haven’t made a decision,” he said on Fox News. “We’ll figure it out sometime next year.”

Allies of Mr. Vance, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, say he is genuinely undecided about his political future. They point to his young family (his fourth child was born in July) as one reason he might not mount a White House bid in 2028. They also note his obsession with political analysis and data and suggest that if he does not see a path to victory, he may sit out this race.

The fallout from the war with Iran — and its unpopularity among voters — could be a significant factor, too. Some allies of Mr. Vance say that if the president decides to resume major combat operations in Iran, it would drastically reduce Mr. Vance’s chances of running.

The vice president, who endorsed Mr. Trump in 2023 saying he would not drag the United States into new wars, expressed reservations about the conflict privately inside the administration. But after the huge G.O.P. losses in this month’s midterms, he went public, laying out in blunt terms what he said went wrong.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in his lengthy social media post the day after the midterms.

Mr. Vance made the point of adding that Mr. Trump had also said as much — though the president has blamed Republicans’ losses on many factors, chiefly that he was not on the ticket.

For Mr. Vance, it appeared to be an attempt to separate himself from the administration’s policy without criticizing the president. But Mr. Trump soon announced that he was pulling his vice president from engaging in peace talks with Iran, an effort that Mr. Vance had intensified shortly before the elections. Mr. Trump said he wanted Mr. Vance to focus on investigating allegations of fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

Alyssa Farah Griffin, who worked in Mr. Trump’s White House during the first term and is now a co-host of “The View,” said that comment from Mr. Vance reminded her of a comment that Kamala Harris, then the vice president, made on the ABC show during the 2024 campaign. When asked if she would have done anything differently from President Joseph R. Biden Jr., Ms. Harris said, “There is not a thing that comes to mind.”

“JD Vance is in the impossible position that any Trump V.P. inevitably ends up in,” Ms. Griffin said. “He can’t have any separation or daylight from the president.”

Mr. Vance’s “daylight” comment this week “may have seemed insignificant in the moment, but it will live in campaign ads,” she added.

Mr. Vance’s allies say a competitive primary, not a coronation, will determine the next Republican presidential nominee, and they cite Ms. Harris’s loss in 2024 as evidence of that theory. Ms. Harris quickly secured the Democratic nomination after Mr. Biden dropped out of the race, despite some Democrats’ calls for a more formal nominating process.

But Mr. Vance ultimately could find himself in a similar situation to Ms. Harris, who many voters saw as an extension of Mr. Biden, political strategists said. Even as she privately signaled she had concerns about Mr. Biden’s handling of the Israel-Hamas war, she was unable to figure out how to separate herself from the unpopular president.

“It’s very hard to get me to say that I have any amount of sympathy for JD Vance because he put himself in this position,” said Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist and former deputy campaign manager to Ms. Harris. “But you do have to feel for him because he’s stuck. When you’re the vice president, you’re stuck. In the Harris situation, there was not much you can actually do to separate yourself.”

Mr. Vance now must wrestle with that complex dynamic as he assesses the future of the Republican Party and in which direction he would try to lead it. His path to the vice presidency — from a “never Trumper” to Mr. Trump’s vice president — suggests that he could go in different directions.

Mr. Vance was an avowed critic of Mr. Trump in 2016, calling him “unfit for our nation’s highest office.” He then became a supporter of Mr. Trump and sought the president’s endorsement when he ran for a Senate seat in Ohio in 2022. He received the endorsement and won that race.

Many Republicans believe Mr. Vance would need the explicit, or at least implicit, support from Mr. Trump to win a Republican primary. But that is far from a guarantee. The president has always relished competition among his aides, and his advisers say he is in no rush to endorse a successor.

And after Republicans’ disastrous results in the elections this month, in which Democrats won the largest midterm victory for either party since the post-Watergate elections, other Republicans see an opening, too. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida are among those considering possible bids.

Then there’s Mr. Rubio. He has said he would support Mr. Vance and dismissed reports that he is going to leave the administration to run for president. But some of his allies said he would run if Mr. Trump encouraged him to do so — and Mr. Trump has not been shy about lavishing praise on him.

“How hot is Marco, right?” Mr. Trump said Tuesday at the ASEAN summit in Manila. “Is Marco doing a great job? He’s been fantastic.”

While Mr. Vance has remained in the United States, as the vice president does when the president travels abroad, Mr. Rubio is playing a prominent role on the president’s trip. On Tuesday, he addressed public fears about the multiple technology outages in the United States, seeking to reassure Americans that there was no evidence of cyberattacks.

Mr. Rubio’s defense of the Iran war, in particular, has earned him good will with the president.

In a recent interview with The Times, Mr. Rubio said Mr. Trump “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for authorizing strikes against Iran.

“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.

The distinct approaches of Mr. Rubio and Mr. Vance underscore a broader debate in the party — should the next Republican presidential candidate align themselves with Mr. Trump’s legacy?

Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey, who himself is considering another run for the White House, said Mr. Vance’s challenges transcend his unique position as vice president.

“I don’t think anyone that was part of Trump 2.0 will be able to win in the fall of 2028,” he said. “They will be billed as another four years of Donald Trump, and that will not be salable to the American people.”

item.title: Senator Bill Cassidy Blocks Trump Pick to Head Science Agency
item.description:
The chairman of the Senate health committee on Wednesday blocked President Trump’s nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, prolonging a leadership vacuum at an agency that has been rocked by the administration’s efforts to reshape research funding.

The committee was scheduled to vote Wednesday on the nomination of Jim O’Neill, a science and technology investor who served briefly as a top deputy to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and had been tapped months ago to lead the science agency.

But moments after convening the committee, the chairman, Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana and fierce critic of Mr. Kennedy, abruptly announced that the panel would not consider Mr. O’Neill’s nomination after all.

A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss a personnel matter, said Mr. Trump had not withdrawn the nomination. It is unclear whether it can move forward without Mr. Cassidy’s support.

Mr. O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science” in previous roles in the administration, Mr. Cassidy said. He noted that several committee members had concerns about Mr. O’Neill’s independent judgment in light of his “role in the firing” of the former director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Susan Monarez.

After Dr. Monarez was pushed out in August 2025, Mr. O’Neill briefly became acting director while continuing to serve as Mr. Kennedy’s deputy. Then he himself was replaced, and nominated to lead the N.S.F. amid a reorganization of the top ranks of the health department.

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Mr. Cassidy said.

The panel’s refusal to consider Mr. O’Neill came just hours after the White House withdrew another Trump nominee. Dr. Heidi Overton, tapped to run the Food and Drug Administration, and Mr. O’Neill were among five nominees to be considered on Wednesday morning. At the last minute, however, the health committee distributed a revised agenda with their names crossed off.

Mr. Cassidy, a physician, lost his primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger and is in his last weeks as a senator. He has faced intense criticism from public health leaders for casting the deciding vote to confirm Mr. Kennedy.

The science foundation, an independent agency that funds basic research, has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since April 2025, when Sethuraman Panchanathan, an appointee from President Trump’s first term, quit amid an administration-led effort to cancel hundreds of active grants and slash agency funding.

In the interim, the Trump administration has sought greater control over the N.S.F. From withholding over $1 billion in congressional appropriations to attempting to defund the social sciences division, the Trump administration has reshaped the agency to align with its priorities.

The changes at the science foundation are part of a broader push by the Trump administration to overhaul federal research funding.

Like some top science officials in the Trump administration, Mr. O’Neill’s background is in venture capital, not science. Mr. O’Neill has a degree in the humanities from Yale University and worked extensively with the Silicon Valley billionaire Peter Thiel before joining the Trump administration.

With Mr. O’Neill’s nomination dashed, it is unclear who will lead the agency next year. Last month, the N.S.F.’s chief of staff, who has led the agency since Dr. Panchanathan quit, announced that he would retire by the end of the year, according to an internal memo reviewed by The New York Times. The N.S.F. declined to comment about its leadership plans.

item.title: Trump Arrives in China Focused on Friendship, Not Spy Scandal
item.description:
President Trump was welcomed to China on Wednesday with a warm embrace both figuratively and literally, as he arrived for a fraught visit shadowed by a major spy scandal that he seemed determined to ignore.

Upon landing in Shenzhen, a bustling technology center, for a series of meetings, Mr. Trump was greeted at the airport by President Xi Jinping of China, who hugged him on a red carpet as a colorfully dressed crowd waved flowers and flags and chanted “warm welcome” in Mandarin.

The visit, however, may have a see-no-evil, hear-no-evil quality because Mr. Trump has said he does not intend to raise the biggest China spy scandal of recent years, one that has upended one of America’s technology giants and pitted members of his own administration against each other. Instead, Mr. Trump prioritized a show of friendship amid the allegations of espionage.

Mr. Trump reveled in the pageantry of the moment as he joined Mr. Xi for a banquet dinner that opened the annual meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a group of 21 major economies in the region. The two leaders toasted future prosperity and looked forward to meeting separately on Thursday as well as together with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in a much-anticipated trilateral summit.

Mr. Xi’s decision to personally welcome Mr. Trump at the airport was a rare act by the Chinese leader. He did not do so when Mr. Trump visited Beijing in May. But Mr. Trump made a point of traveling to Joint Base Andrews outside Washington to greet Mr. Xi in September, an uncommon move for an American president and the first time Mr. Trump had done so for a foreign visitor.

So, Mr. Xi returned the gesture on Wednesday. “China is a nation of etiquette with a tradition of reciprocity,” Mr. Xi said, according to Chinese state media.

By contrast, Mr. Xi sent lower-level officials to greet Mr. Putin and other regional leaders arriving for the summit meeting, as is customary.

Still, Mr. Xi met separately with Mr. Putin for more than two hours in advance of the three-way meeting planned for Thursday, and he hailed the Chinese-Russian relationship as “steadfast as a rock through wind and rain.”

The two encounters underscored Mr. Xi’s efforts to balance relations with Russia and the United States. While Russia has become a close partner in recent years and Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin have developed a bond over dozens of meetings, China has a far more extensive and important economic relationship with the United States.

The atmosphere at the summit with other leaders was sometimes tense. Mr. Xi barely offered a smile to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan, with whom he is in a bitter, yearlong diplomatic spat. Mr. Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, who have an uneasy relationship as they tussle over trade, had their first in-person meeting of the year. Days earlier, Mr. Carney angered the Trump administration by repeating that he would look elsewhere, including to China, if Mr. Trump did not lift tariffs on Canada’s auto exports.

Left unaddressed was the recent revelation that Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, had an extramarital affair with a business executive who U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The executive, Alice Huang, who is not related, worked for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center firm and was suspected of gathering intelligence for Beijing.

Mr. Huang resigned under pressure and Mr. Trump’s senior advisers have been squabbling over administration policy on chip exports that could benefit China. The administration announced earlier this week new rules meant to restrict remote access to advanced chips and servers that could help develop Chinese artificial intelligence.

Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, has blamed Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, for resisting restrictions on chip sales. Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick are both accompanying Mr. Trump on his Asia trip, though they were seen standing apart. .

The Nvidia scandal has put Mr. Trump on the defensive because of his close relationship with Mr. Huang, who joined the president’s trip to China in May. Mr. Trump has denied being told about the matter, despite reporting by The New York Times that he was informed at least twice, including en route to China in May. He has said he does not know if Ms. Huang was a spy and urged Mr. Huang to fight for his job. Even after Mr. Huang’s resignation, Mr. Trump voiced support for his reinstatement.

This is not the first time Mr. Trump has opted not to confront Mr. Xi with allegations of Chinese interference in the sensitive U.S. matters. In a prime-time address to the nation in July, Mr. Trump accused China of hacking or purchasing U.S. voter rolls, but then said nothing about it publicly when he hosted Mr. Xi for a lavish state visit at the White House in September.

Although Mr. Trump once regularly lashed out at China over its trade practices, he has become more intent over the past year on forging closer ties between the world’s two largest economies. “We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them,” he said before leaving the United States.

Mr. Trump arrived in China after a stop in Manila for the annual meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN. He met with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, who engaged in some fast-food diplomacy with the American president, who is known for his taste for greasy meals.

Mr. Marcos said that he sent some fried chicken to Mr. Trump at his hotel the night before from Jollibee, a chain that is considered a national treasure in the Philippines. “Since you’re strapped for time, I thought a taste of Manila might be good,” he said. Mr. Trump did not say whether he ate the food.

He did, however, make a point of paying a visit to Mr. Marcos’s mother, Imelda Marcos, 97, the former first lady of the Philippines, who got to know Mr. Trump at New York parties in the 1990s.

“Welcome to the Philippines,” she told Mr. Trump. She handed him a gift and blew him a kiss as he walked away with her son.

“She’s always the most beautiful,” Mr. Trump said.

While Mr. Trump failed to sign a trade deal with Thailand that had been expected to be finalized during his stop in Manila, he announced that he did unexpectedly reach a trade agreement with the Philippines. “We didn’t know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it’s a magnificent deal for both,” he said.

Mr. Marcos’s office later said the deal would cover energy and food security, without providing further details. Mr. Trump said on social media that the deal would benefit American farmers.

There was no such accord between Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney after their tense encounter in Shenzhen later in the day. In a statement, Mr. Carney’s office said that the two leaders “discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement” but offered no further details.

Much attention was focused on Mr. Trump’s meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday. The White House said Mr. Trump will also meet separately with Mr. Putin, their first get-together since a much-ballyhooed Alaska summit failed to produce an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

Mr. Putin arrived in Asia with a show of force. Even as he landed in Shenzhen, Russian strategic nuclear bombers landed in Vietnam. It was the first time that Russian strategic nuclear bombers had deployed to Vietnam since the Soviet era and served as a reminder before the trilateral talks that Moscow remains the world’s largest nuclear power.

Reporting was contributed by Paul Sonne, Ian Austen and Keith Bradsher in Shenzhen; Lily Kuo in Taipei, Taiwan; Leo Sands in London; Aie Balagtas See in Manila; and Francesca Regalado.

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin Will Sit Down for the First Time. It Won’t Be Like Yalta.
item.description:
The meeting Thursday between President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir V. Putin marks the first time in history that the leaders of the United States, China and Russia — possessors of more than 90 percent of the world’s nuclear weapons — have sat down together.

But not every first in history results in a significant accomplishment — or any accomplishment. And as Mr. Trump landed on late Wednesday in Shenzhen, the chip-making, telecommunications, software and robotics heart of China, it was already clear that this meeting was unlikely to live up to the many comparisons being made to Yalta, the end-of-World-War-II conference where Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin divided up the globe.

Together, talking largely in secret, the Yalta participants laid the foundation for a postwar order that lasted nearly half a century, while leaving millions of people trapped behind the Iron Curtain.

There are many reasons that Yalta is a poor analog when thinking about the Shenzhen summit. Yalta stretched over eight days, with a bevy of diplomats and generals working the back rooms to turn the visions discussed by the three leaders into action plans. The meeting involving Mr. Trump, Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi is set to last around an hour or so — essentially a glorified photo op, by comparison, and not one in which major issues are likely to be settled.

And instead of a conclave of three allies on the verge of a joint victory over a mutual foe, this meeting features three leaders who have not been partners in a great venture, and are unlikely to be any time soon.

The three men have major differences on issues as far-ranging as China’s fast-growing nuclear arsenal, the regulation of artificial intelligence, the future of space weapons, the war in Ukraine and the war in Iran — a conflict that has haunted Mr. Trump, enriched Mr. Putin and angered Mr. Xi.

So they will not enter the room expecting that they will have time to raise, much less resolve, many critical issues.

But even photo ops can linger as important symbols. And the one that may appeal to all three men is the message that they are the true global deciders, engaged in a project to shape world order.

After enduring a resounding electoral defeat this month, that image may be particularly appealing to Mr. Trump, who makes no secret of his admiration for strong leaders who do not have to put up with pesky legislatures or an intrusive press.

For Mr. Putin, the meeting serves to help readmit him to the world community, and to recognize that he remains too powerful to ignore, even after losing half a million soldiers in a nearly five-year-long battle for Ukraine.

And Mr. Xi gets to play the role of global convener, albeit of a gathering with an exclusive list of participants.

Among those not at the table: Japan, India, South Korea, Australia, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Brazil, Canada, Mexico, South Africa and, perhaps most notably, Ukraine and Iran.

Still, Mr. Trump, Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi clearly have conflicting agendas. Mr. Trump has repeatedly said in recent days that his No. 1 priority is to take on “denuclearization,” his somewhat sloppy way of referring to arms control. Mr. Putin likely wants to talk about Ukraine, potentially figuring that Mr. Trump wants a peace deal and will not be especially picky about the details.

And Mr. Xi, who was wary about holding any meeting without a predetermined outcome, will be looking for ways to leverage his role in the service of becoming the world’s largest military, economic and technological power by 2049 — the 100th year of Mao’s revolution.

The three men have deeply complicated relationships. The Chinese and Russian presidents have met roughly 50 times, and famously declared five years ago a “partnership without limits.” While that partnership falls well short of a true alliance, they are unified in a mutual desire to diminish the scope of American power. That was evident on Wednesday, when Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin met together.

In their one-on-one conversation, Mr. Xi told the Russian leader, who he has at times referred to as his greatest friend, that relations between China and Russia had remained as “steadfast as a rock through wind and rain,” according to Chinese state media. Mr. Xi called for the two sides to advance the “democratization of international relations,” a term he often uses to describe a world order in which the United States is less dominant.

For his part, Mr. Putin appears happy to possibly be perceived as out of the penalty box for his brutal invasion of Ukraine.

“He’s at the big boys table with the other great superpowers,” said Alina Polyakova, the president of the Center for European Policy Analysis. “For Putin, it’s credibility, it’s legitimacy. He sees himself as the tsar of an empire rather than the president of a frankly declining” country.

Mr. Trump’s national security policy refers to an updated “Monroe Doctrine” aimed at keeping foreign powers out of the Western Hemisphere. Mr. Putin talks about restoring much of the empire of Peter the Great, starting with Ukraine — but perhaps not ending there. Mr. Xi has expanded his military operations in the Pacific, building bases out of artificial islands in the South China Sea, confronting the Philippines over ownership of some of its islands, and running near-constant military exercises that encircle Taiwan.

It all feels very much like the late 1800s, the peak of the “spheres of influence” approach to world governance by a few dominant nations. In January, asked whether he believed in a spheres-of-influence approach to the world, Mr. Trump said, “It’s not necessarily where I want it to go.” But he added that as he looked around the world, “it’s where it’s going.”

It is clear that none of the three superpowers want to be limited to their own neighborhoods, even if their maps are expansively drawn. China may be focused on the Pacific first, but it wants access to copper mines in Peru and Ecuador. The United States may talk the talk of withdrawing from the world, but it wants to retain influence across the Middle East, which is why it has kept the bases that Iran attacked in the Gulf in recent months, forcing some to all but shutter. And it is not about to give up its presence in Japan or South Korea.

Russia has ambitions that also reach into space and cyberspace, as well as the Arctic and Africa.

Still, there is a serious imbalance among the three nations that will be represented at the meeting. While the United States and China are the two leading global powers, Russia pales by comparison in most respects, other than its residual nuclear arsenal and its energy resources.

While the United States and China are racing to develop artificial intelligence, Russia is at best a bit player in that field. Other than its nuclear capacity, Russia’s military has been shown over the past four years to be far weaker than Mr. Putin projected.

And economically, Russia cannot compete with the other two countries at the table. While the United States and China are the world’s largest and second-largest economies, respectively, Russia places only eighth. Its economy is barely one-eighth of the size of China’s, and one-eleventh the size of the United States’. It manufactures almost nothing of value for much of the rest of the world, other than military hardware — and vodka and caviar.

So for Mr. Putin, the meeting allows him to project the illusion that he and his country are more important than they actually are, to claim a certain geopolitical swagger unjustified by reality.

The meeting is also a way for Mr. Putin to snub Europe and essentially say that he does not need to deal with those countries, because he can sit down with the leaders of the two most important powers in the world.

“Demonstrating Europe’s irrelevance is very important to Putin at this point,” said Michael Kimmage, the director of the Kennan Institute, named for George Kennan, the famed American diplomat who designed much of the strategy around the Cold War.

“I think nothing is going to come of it, and it will be fairly quickly forgotten,” he added. “But still, to go from the Treaty of Versailles to Yalta to this shows that Europe is being erased.”

Ukraine may be discussed, as Mr. Trump indicated shortly before leaving the United States for Asia. But many Americans and Europeans close to the peace talks have concluded that Mr. Putin has no interest in making a deal to end the war. His government’s current proposal largely repeats the same maximalist demands it made before the full-scale invasion of 2022, conditions that were unacceptable to Europe and Ukraine then and remain so today.

Michael McFaul, a former ambassador to Russia, said Mr. Putin had made plain he was not seeking peace. “If he really thought this was an event for peace, the last thing he would be doing would be bombing the bridges in Kyiv that is now crippling the capital of Ukraine,” Mr. McFaul said. “I don’t think he thinks of this as a genuine effort to advance peace. He gets the photo op and he gets to call it Yalta 2.0.”

Still, some foreign policy veterans said that the meeting could not hurt — and in some ways, could probably help — by opening lines of communication among three powers that are crucial to issues around the globe.

“Even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile,” Charles Kupchan, a Georgetown international affairs professor and former national security aide to Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, wrote in Foreign Affairs. “Trump, Xi and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.”

item.title: New Members Get a Congress Crash Course With Grade School Vibes
item.description:
The classmates lined up shoulder-to-shoulder on the Capitol steps, with the taller ones in the back and shorter peers up front. Some blinked and others frowned, but most smiled ear-to-ear as a photographer took their class picture on a recent overcast morning during their visit to Washington.

These were not grade schoolers on a field trip, or interns on their first day of work. They were a large and diverse group of full-fledged adults elected two weeks ago to serve in Congress and who, come January, will be its newest members.

They were in the nation’s capital for new-member orientation, a biennial crash course in legislating, office-managing and all manner of other tasks that come with the job. The House newcomers, of which at least 75 are Democrats and 32 are Republicans, have been spending their days wandering the halls of the Capitol wearing orientation lanyards fastened to name tags.

They attend trainings with titles ranging from “Constituent Services 101” to “What Is a Member’s Job?” In the evenings, they hobnob with their colleagues at dinners and receptions.

On picture day, the representatives-elect roared in applause after their group photograph, and then scattered across the Capitol steps to sort themselves into various cliques for close-ups. Female veterans posed together, flexing their muscles. Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York linked arms as they posed with other democratic socialists elected this month. Florida Republicans made alligator-chomping hand gestures for the camera.

Victoria Broderick, a Tennessee Democrat who made the trip even though her race against Representative Scott DesJarlais, a Republican, remained too close to call, climbed onto the balcony and threw her hands up in the air for a solo shot.

It was a bit like the first week of school, and many members of the new congressional class documented their newbie status on social media. But instead of classes, these attendees were requesting committee assignments. In place of tutors, they were choosing legislative advisers. And in lieu of essay writing, they learned the mechanics of bill drafting.

“It feels like a week ago, I was running around my state in jeans and a sweatshirt, knocking doors and talking to people,” Representative-elect Denise Powell, Democrat of Nebraska, said on her way to a Democratic soiree outside the House chamber. “And now I’m here, and it’s kind of hard to process. But, man, it’s just so exciting.”

Over the past several days, 105 representatives-elect have been schooled on the basics: where to live, whom to hire, what to buy. (The 19 senators-elect have a separate, less structured orientation program but have also been in Washington getting acclimated to the job they are about to take on.)

Representative-elect Kristina Knickerbocker, Democrat of Ohio, said she had gone on runs around Washington to get to know the city, parts of which are deceptively hilly. Delegate-elect Janelle Sarauw, Democrat of the U.S. Virgin Islands, said she would need a down jacket now that she will be working in Washington.

“It’s just one season for the entire year in the Virgin Islands,” Ms. Sarauw said.

At the Capitol as at a new school, there are plenty of complex social dynamics to navigate. By the end of the training, each party chooses a class president. Loose factions form. Republicans, whose class is tiny compared with that of Democrats because of the G.O.P.’s sweeping losses, appeared to be hanging out mostly with other Republicans. Much attention was paid to the youngsters who had made waves before arriving — Ms. Avila-Chevalier, Ms. Valdez and Melat Kiros, their fellow democratic socialist from Colorado, walked around with a semi-permanent entourage of reporters.

Some of the fashion statements that gained notoriety on the campaign trail have made their way back to Washington, such as Senators-elect Roy Cooper and Scott Colom wearing Air Jordans when they arrived in the Senate.

And popular classmates emerge, such as Mr. Colom, who will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, and Representative-elect Bobby Pulido, a Latin Grammy Award-winning Tejano singer recently elected from Texas.

“Being able to serve now in Congress with someone like Congressman Bobby Pulido, who I grew up listening to, that to me is a very surreal experience,” said Representative-elect Patty García, Democrat of Illinois.

There are also rites of passage, like on Tuesday, when the soon-to-be freshmen gathered in the underground room beneath the Capitol to pull numbers out of a wooden box for the congressional room lottery. But instead of picking a dorm, they were choosing offices.

Lawmakers were summoned one by one to draw a numbered chip from a box to determine the order in which they would make their office selection, a ritual that began in 1908 when politicians needed to settle who would get what room in what is now the Cannon House Office Building.

On Tuesday, the classmates hollered and cheered each other on as each approached the storied box that had disappointed and delighted so many of their predecessors. John Cowan, Republican of Georgia and a neurosurgeon, wore his lucky white coat. He scored No. 11. Fredrick Haynes, Democrat of Texas, took a bow after picking No. 19 out of the lot.

Representative-elect Houston Gaines, another Georgia Republican, picked No. 67, and in true grade-school fashion, moved his hands up and down in Gen Z’s universal gesture for the “6-7” meme that might have been lost on many of his older colleagues.

Shannon Taylor, a Virginia Democrat, walked up apprehensively to meet her bureaucratic fate.

“This is so nerve-racking,” she cried, lowering her hand into the box.

The Democrat opened her eyes and peeked at her chip. With a gasp, Ms. Taylor said, beaming: “Oh my god, I’m 1!”

It was also her birthday, prompting a collective rendition of “Happy Birthday” from the class. She chose a spacious fourth-floor space in the Rayburn House Office Building, despite its structural woes.

Mark Teixeira, Republican of Texas, winced when he saw his bad luck; he had drawn No. 105, dead last, and would be relegated to a ground-floor space in the Longworth Building.

Then Mr. Texeira, who spent eight years as a first baseman with the New York Yankees, laughed at his own misfortune, stretching his arms wide as his classmates gave him a lengthy standing ovation. They gave him high-fives in a dugout-style line as he returned to his seat.

item.title: Ground Stop Came as Duffy Pushed to Rapidly Upgrade Aviation Systems
item.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration’s decision to upgrade communications equipment on Friday afternoon, leading to a halt in air travel during one of the busiest times of the week, reflects the breakneck pace of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s efforts to overhaul the country’s aviation infrastructure.

“The longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes,” Mr. Duffy told reporters Tuesday on Capitol Hill. “So we do have to charge forward.”

But current and former officials say Mr. Duffy’s push to transform the F.A.A.’s slow and cautious culture — including by rapidly installing artificial intelligence systems and finishing upgrades before President Trump leaves office — is a risky gambit that could continue to disrupt air traveland lead to other fallout.

Federal officials are still trying to determine how the replacement of wiring at a remote facility in Arkansas may have led to a data overload in critical air traffic control systems across the country on Friday. As the technical problems caused radio static in communications between pilots and air traffic controllers, the F.A.A. grounded all flights, imposing the longest nationwide halt since the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

The very fact that such work was being done on a Friday afternoon was imprudent, according to some federal aviation experts.

“During the time that I was at the F.A.A., if we were doing any change, we would try to do it at an off-peak period,” said Katie Thomson, Maryland’s transportation secretary, who served as the F.A.A.’s No. 2 official under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. She added, “It would not be something that we would do on a Friday afternoon at peak travel hours.”

Mary Schiavo, a former Transportation Department inspector general during the first Bush and Clinton administrations, said that while the nation urgently needed to modernize its air traffic control system, performing the upgrade on a busy Friday afternoon suggested that it was moving too quickly.

“That’s not typical. Everyone knows that’s a busy travel time,” she said in an interview. “I would imagine the looming Thanksgiving holiday had them on overdrive.”

The upgrade was done on a Friday afternoon instead of at night or over the weekend in order to meet the project’s ambitious schedule, and because the work was not considered high risk, according to a person with knowledge of the agency’s investigation who was not authorized to speak publicly.

Officials still have not determined the root cause of the failure that led to the ground stop, which was only the third one in the agency’s history. The incident led to thousands of delays ahead of the busy holiday travel season and deepened worries about the safety of the nation’s aviation system, which has experienced a cascade of problems in recent years including last year’s midair collision above Washington, D.C., that killed 67 people.

Mr. Duffy has said no travelers were in danger on Friday and that there is no evidence of sabotage. He has said the incident showed the need for vast new investments in the aviation communications systems. But the situation has raised questions about the transportation secretary’s stewardship of the aviation system, including whether the pace of upgrades was pushing work to be done at times that pose a high risk of travel disruptions.

Mr. Duffy told reporters on Saturday that officials did not anticipate that Friday’s upgrades, which were conducted at a small, remote facility in El Dorado, Ark., could threaten the entire network, and that contractors regularly did such work at remote locations during the day.

“These smaller locations don’t have that kind of impact — or they shouldn’t have that kind of impact,” he said, adding that “there’ll be a re-evaluation of when we do this work.”

The job, in which copper wire used for telecommunications was being upgraded to fiber-optic cable, was performed between about 10 a.m. and 3 p.m., according to the F.A.A.

But shortly after the work, a router that had just been installed began firing a barrage of data that overloaded critical air traffic control systems at locations around the country. As some pilots began noticing radio static in their conversations with air traffic controllers, federal officials moved to ground all planes at 3:54 p.m.

The Arkansas upgrade was being handled by a single technician employed by L3Harris, one of the F.A.A.’s biggest contractors, officials have said. The work had been approved by the agency and was supervised by one of its technicians, Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, told reporters on Tuesday. Similar work had been completed many times at other locations with no major issues, Mr. Bedford said.

Mr. Duffy said in a recent interview on CNBC that he could not “guarantee” that future disruptions would now happen without continued investment.

Mr. Duffy has demanded $50 billion in additional funding, a request that caused lawmakers, including some Republicans, to recoil on Tuesday. The F.A.A. has so far spent a small fraction of the $12.5 billion Congress appropriated for air traffic modernization last year. Transportation Department officials say they have committed about a third of the funding earmarked for telecommunications and radar upgrades.

Officials say 70 percent of the network’s copper wires have been replaced with high-speed fiber-optic cables. About half of the cables were upgraded in the past year alone, a considerably faster pace than previous administrations have reached.

But experts previously warned that the faster pace has potential downsides. A report in September by the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan federal watchdog agency, noted both advantages and risks of Mr. Duffy’s expedited improvements.

The Trump administration shaved roughly nine years off its timeline to modernize voice radio systems used by air traffic controllers, the report said. It also sped up the replacement of copper wire with fiber by 21 months.

But at the same time, the faster pace carried the potential of “cost increases and potential disruptions to the national airspace,” said Kevin Walsh, the director of information technology and cybersecurity audits for the G.A.O., in an interview with The New York Times.

The F.A.A.’s telecommunications network and its hardware issues were a trouble spot for domestic air travel long before travel came to a halt on Friday.

In April 2025, air traffic controllers handling flights in and out of Newark Liberty International Airport experienced a simultaneous outage of their radar feeds and their radio contact with pilots because of a burned copper wire, a Transportation Department inspector general inquiry found. And as recently as September, a technical glitch at a Philadelphia air traffic hub and the cutting of a fiber backup line interrupted controller communications in the Northeast Corridor.

Given that about 30 percent of the country’s aviation data lines still run through copper wires, additional, and potentially ill-timed, upgrades may be in store.

And as the F.A.A. works through a new and more ambitious operating pace, the Trump administration has tried to bring in fresh ideas and systems to help.

Those attempts have also faced problems.

In December 2025, the F.A.A. used a competitive bidding process to hire the security technology company Peraton to manage the air traffic control system overhaul, for which Congress had set aside $12.5 billion in funding.

The idea was for Peraton’s team to offer expertise and coordinate the network of contractors that would install the needed hardware and software. But Peraton’s team faced resistance from F.A.A. employees, some of whom thought that team lacked the expertise to take over agency work, said a former F.A.A. employee and three other people with knowledge of the matter. The people requested anonymity to discuss confidential processes.

Peraton was under a tight timeline — one that has been strained at times because of limits on access to facilities and delivery schedules, according to one of these people.

Peraton spokespeople did not respond to requests for comment.

Other contractors and timelines have encountered pushback from F.A.A. employees, according to current and former F.A.A. and Transportation Department employees.

An artificial intelligence system meant to optimize the routing of flights in and out of U.S. airports to account for weather, neighboring traffic and other factors has been one such effort, said three people who were briefed on the matter but requested anonymity to discuss confidential proceedings.

Known as Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART, the new system was rolled out in September at Washington-area airports by Air Space Intelligence, a Boston tech company that was awarded an $875 million contract in June.

But the system faced opposition from Shawn McClosky, the air traffic manager running the F.A.A. airspace command center in Warrenton, Va., said the four people who were briefed on the matter. Mr. McClosky believed the system was being launched too hastily and without proper review, two of those people said.

His supervisor, LaKisha Price, a senior system operations manager at the F.A.A., backed Mr. McClosky up, the people said, pushing for additional reviews. Both were removed from their positions.

Ms. Price and officials at Air Space Intelligence did not respond to requests for comment. Mr. McClosky declined to comment.

Julie Tate contributed research.

item.title: Judge Keeps in Place Block on Construction of Trump’s Triumphal Arch
item.description:
A federal judge on Wednesday extended an order prohibiting the Trump administration from breaking ground on a triumphal arch in Washington that the president has said would be built in his honor.

In a brief five-page order, Judge Tanya S. Chutkan wrote that there was good reason to preserve the status quo at the site, which sits over the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial, while she weighed the competing interests in the case. The decision came as new parties, including relatives of former President John F. Kennedy as well as Virginia and the District of Columbia, have recently joined a group of veterans in bringing legal challenges to the project.

Judge Chutkan had previously blocked construction earlier this month, with an order that had been set to expire on Thursday. Her new order blocks construction through Dec. 2, prohibiting the government from “initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity” associated with the project.

The 250-foot triumphal arch President Trump has proposed building near Arlington National Cemetery stands out as one of his few ideas for Washington that has yet to have work begun in earnest. Projects at the White House, the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are all underway.

A small group of veterans had sued to halt the project in February, arguing that its height and proximity to the military cemetery would block views and diminish the sanctity of the grounds. Last month, Arlington County also sued, citing practical concerns.

A later suit by Virginia and the District of Columbia raised concerns similar to Arlington’s, including traffic disruptions and budgetary pressure from accommodating the construction.

Members of the Kennedy family have said the giant arch could also cast a shadow on the gravesite of the former president, which sits at the heart of Arlington National Cemetery.

Judges have sought to block even preliminary work on Trump’s projects, wary that, if allowed, the federal government could make irreversible changes before lawsuits challenging the projects can be heard in full.

Earlier this month, a federal judge barred the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park in Washington, after finding that the proposed closure and an earlier removal of trees appeared to be preparation for turning the space into a professional golf course that Mr. Trump has sought.

item.title: Fight Over Deportation Protections for Venezuelans Returns to Supreme Court
item.description:
The Trump administration on Wednesday asked the Supreme Court to intervene before deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans could be reinstated later this week.

The justices previously allowed the administration to move forward with its plans to end the protections for more than 300,000 Venezuelan immigrants who had been living legally in the United States under the program known as Temporary Protected Status.

But the court’s earlier ruling in 2025 came in an emergency order. That meant it was technically temporary, lasting only while litigation over the issue continued in the lower courts.

That litigation has continued to move forward. A district court judge had initially ruled in September 2025 that Kristi Noem, then the homeland security secretary, had exceeded her authority when she ended deportation protections for Venezuelans. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit recently paused that ruling but did not overturn it. The pause is set to expire on Friday.

On Wednesday, D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, raced to the Supreme Court and urged the justices to step in quickly. If it does not, he said the Venezuelans will suddenly be able to claim status under the program for the first time in 19 months, allowing them access to the ability to live and work in the United States without fear of deportation. That outcome, he wrote, would “visit acute harm on the government and the public interest and foment chaos.”

Emi MacLean, an attorney at the A.C.L.U. of Northern California, accused the administration of “gamesmanship” and trying to “jump the line” before the appeals court has had an opportunity to rule on the status of the protections for Venezuelans.

The Trump administration has broadly pushed to terminate the Temporary Protected Status program as part of its efforts to restrict immigration. Congress created T.P.S. with bipartisan support in 1990 to provide temporary legal status to people whose home countries were deemed unsafe because of war, natural disasters or other crises.

In two separate cases in June, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority allowed the Trump administration to end humanitarian protections that had permitted people from Haiti and Syria to live and work legally in the United States for more than a decade. Writing for the majority, Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. said the federal law at issue prohibited courts from second-guessing an administration’s determination to end deportation protections.

“This text is clear, and its plain meaning is very broad,” he wrote.

After that decision, the justices sent the case involving Venezuelans back to the Ninth Circuit to reconsider in light of the ruling. Mr. Sauer said that same reasoning the court used to judge the issue for people from Haiti and Syria should apply in the pending case.

Reinstating protections now, the administration told the justices on Wednesday, would be “enormously disruptive” and could require the government to release an estimated 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, according to the Trump administration’s filing.

For months, Venezuelans have been among the hundreds of thousands of T.P.S. holders plunged into legal uncertainty as the Trump administration has sought to terminate the form of humanitarian protections.

Lawyers have said hundreds of Venezuelans have already been detained and deported, with some parents separated from their American-born children. Some have been scrambling to find other forms of immigration protection, including asylum, that might allow them access to work visas. But the pathways are narrow, and petitions can take years to process.

Jazmine Ulloa contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Weighs New Strikes on Iran as Israel Presses for Action, Officials Say
item.description:
President Trump is weighing plans for another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, taking into account new intelligence about Iranian capabilities and intensifying pressure from Israel to move quickly and aggressively, U.S. and Israeli officials briefed on the discussions said.

Mr. Trump has yet to make a decision, they said. But he has been considering warnings from Israel about Iran’s success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.

And he is taking into account that the United States now has a window in which it has significant military firepower in the region.

There are deep differences of opinion within the administration about the strength of the intelligence and the wisdom of assaulting Iran again, especially after a midterm election in which voters clearly expressed displeasure with a war that has driven up prices and failed to yield the quick triumph that Mr. Trump had promised at its outset, nearly eight months ago.

But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, whose hold on his job is especially tenuous after elections there last month, is pressing hard for the United States to join his country in a four- to seven-day campaign of airstrikes against Iran, the people briefed on the discussions said. The officials spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive security issues.

The conversations intensified last week. Roman Gofman, the director of Mossad, the Israeli intelligence agency, held meetings in Washington, including with the C.I.A. director, John Ratcliffe. Other top Israeli officials, including Shlomi Binder, the director of military intelligence, have advocated a resumption of operations in discussions with American counterparts.

A senior Israeli official disputed the notion that Mr. Netanyahu had pressured Mr. Trump. A spokesman for Mr. Netanyahu said the prime minister had always acted to “safeguard the security” of Israel.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly vacillated in recent months about restarting major combat. He has declared at times that the war is over and suggested at others that he could strike again to ensure that Iran could never develop a nuclear weapon.

He recently instructed Vice President JD Vance to abandon an effort to reach a negotiated solution, and has appeared to embrace the idea that a prolonged economic squeeze would eventually lead Iran to seek a deal under which it would give up its nuclear program.

But Mr. Trump is also highly sensitive to the criticism that the United States has in effect lost the war, people familiar with his thinking said. And after spending two years flexing executive power, the president is entering a lame-duck period of his second term. He has often used shows of force when he has faced pushback or uncertainty in the past.

A U.S. official said Mr. Trump no longer needed to conduct major combat against Iran because his economic pressure campaign had devastated the country.

But the official added that Mr. Trump had all options available to ensure that Iran could never have a nuclear weapon.

In recent weeks, the U.S. military has built up an especially vast arsenal in the region, with naval ships, fighter planes and bombers ready to launch a relatively short campaign of intense strikes against Iran’s drone and missile arsenal, as well as Iranian energy facilities, should Mr. Trump authorize action, military officials said.

That force briefly grew earlier this week with the arrival in the region of a third aircraft carrier, the U.S.S. Theodore Roosevelt. That marked only the second time the United States has had three carriers in the Middle East since the Iraq war in 2003. But just as quickly, one of the other carriers, the U.S.S. George Washington, headed back to the Pacific.

Dozens of fighter jets and attack planes based in the Middle East would join any strike, as would long-range B-1 and B-2 bombers in the United States, which for weeks have been on 96-hour notice for possible missions against Iran.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, have presented the president with a menu of military options that Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command, developed in recent months. Admiral Cooper is traveling in the region this week, U.S. officials said.

Given the possibility of major combat restarting, the Pentagon and State Department have withdrawn personnel from bases and facilities in the region as a precaution. The United States also recently delivered an additional Patriot antimissile battery to Israel, military officials said.

The Pentagon declined to comment on Wednesday, citing operational security. It added in a statement that “the U.S. military continues to provide the president options, and all options remain on the table.”

The C.I.A. also declined to comment.

Any U.S. strikes would likely focus on Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, much of which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps has rebuilt since the early phase of the war, military officials said. Other targets could include Iranian energy facilities and Revolutionary Guards command posts and headquarters.

Israel’s planning has also encompassed further attacks on Iranian nuclear sites and, most provocatively, widespread strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure that could cut off power to industry and civilians, something that Mr. Trump has yet to agree to, people familiar with the discussions said.

From the start of the war, Mr. Netanyahu has pushed plans that he insists could instill a popular uprising against the government, something that has yet to show any signs of coming to pass.

For the Israeli prime minister, the push for another round of strikes is inextricably tied to his fight for political survival. Following last month’s election in Israel, Mr. Netanyahu remains at the head of a caretaker government as a coalition of opposition parties is seeking to form a government. Renewed fighting could delay or derail the opposition’s attempt to form a government and create pressure for a unity government that would include Mr. Netanyahu.

In seeking to convince the United States to join in another round of major attacks, Israel has highlighted what it contends are a variety of threats from Tehran. Israeli officials have been asserting that Iran continues to possess significant chemical and biological weapon capabilities that pose a regional threat — and that could be used in terrorist attacks against the U.S. and Europe.

They have also suggested that the Iranians are able to equip drones in the region with some of those weapons, and use them to strike Israel or its neighbors.

People briefed on the discussions said that U.S. intelligence officials also see evidence of stepped-up efforts by Iran to bolster its chemical and biological weapon capacities.

But they said the prevailing view is that Iran is doing so not to use those weapons preemptively against Israel and other foes, but to deter the United States and Israel from employing nuclear weapons or conducting large-scale attacks that would inflict substantial damage on Iran’s infrastructure or civilians.

The Israelis have shared intelligence claiming that Iranians have plotted to use chemical agents against senior U.S. officials. One person briefed on the intelligence, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said that type of threat was related to the decision in recent weeks to move Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent from his home.

Mark Mazzetti contributed reporting.
